lesson.title: Wide Open: The Astonishing Voltage Gain Inside a Bare Op-Amp
lesson.summary: Open-loop gain is the enormous, largely unregulated voltage gain an operational amplifier provides with no external feedback connected, and its sheer size is both the source of the op-amp's power and the reason it cannot be used raw.
lesson.body:
An operational amplifier is built around a differential input stage: it has two input terminals, a non-inverting input (V+) and an inverting input (V-), and it amplifies the difference between them. With no feedback path connecting the output back to either input, the amplifier is said to be operating open-loop, and its output obeys Vout = A_OL times (V+ minus V-), where A_OL is the open-loop gain, essentially the amplifier gain from the previous chapter, but specific to the op-amp's internal design with feedback removed.

Real op-amps have open-loop gains that are difficult to appreciate intuitively. A classic general-purpose part such as the 741 has an open-loop voltage gain around 200,000, and many modern precision op-amps exceed a million. Datasheets often quote this in decibels instead, since 200,000 corresponds to roughly 20 log10(200,000), which is about 106 dB.

To see how sensitive this makes the output, suppose the differential input voltage, V+ minus V-, is a mere 50 microvolts, or 0.00005 volts, smaller than the thermal noise present in many circuits. With A_OL = 200,000, the predicted output is Vout = 0.00005 V times 200,000 = 10 V.

This is exactly the problem with using open-loop gain directly: 10 volts of output from only 50 microvolts of input differential means the amplifier is absurdly sensitive to its input. Push the differential input just a little higher, say to 100 microvolts, and the predicted output becomes 0.0001 V times 200,000 = 20 V, a value that exceeds the supply rails of most op-amp circuits and simply cannot be produced. The real amplifier does not output 20 V, it saturates, or clips, at whatever voltage its power supply allows, typically a volt or two below the supply rail. Worse, A_OL itself is not a precise, stable number, it varies with temperature, supply voltage, and from one manufactured unit to the next, sometimes by a factor of two or more.

So open-loop gain, despite being the raw source of an op-amp's amplifying power, is far too large and far too unpredictable to use directly in a working circuit. The next two chapters address this from two directions: first by formalizing the idealized model of the op-amp that circuit designers use for analysis, and then by showing how wrapping the amplifier in negative feedback tames this wild open-loop gain into something precise and controllable.
